newsitem.title: INDIA: South Asian states call for trade, investment ties.
newsitem.headline: South Asian states call for trade, investment ties.

text.p: South Asian nations on Monday called for increased cooperation in trade, reductions in tariffs and the promotion of investment in the region.

"Free trade is the mechanism by which we will be able to improve the common welfare (of all South Asian nations)," Bangladesh's Commerce Secretary, Syed A.F. Choudhury, told a business meeting of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) in the Indian capital.

SAARC comprises the Himalayan kingdoms of Bhutan and Nepal, the Indian Ocean island nations of the Maldives and Sri Lanka, mostly Hindu India and its Moslem majority neighbours, Bangladesh and Pakistan.
SAARC took the first steps towards forming a trade bloc in 1995 with the creation of the South Asian Preferential Trading Arrangement (SAPTA), vowing to form a free-trade zone by the year 2005.
"We need to dismantle trade barriers," Choudhury said. "Otherwise, movement from SAPTA to SAFTA will be slow."
SAFTA is the South Asian Free Trade Area planned by the member countries to start operating by the year 2000.
Choudhury said Bangladesh in the recent years had eased import restrictions and reduced tariffs which had helped India to increase its exports to Bangladesh.
"India has emerged as the largest exporter to Bangladesh in the recent past," Choudhury said.
Nepal's Commerce Secretary S.N. Upadhaya urged business leaders from other South Asian nations to invest in Nepal in the tourism and hydro power sectors.
"Nepal offers vast potential in tourism and hydro power sectors," Upadhaya said. He said Nepal had the potential to generate thousands of megawatts of electricity.
Indian Commerce Secretary P.P. Prabhu said easing of restrictions in the areas of visas, transportation and tourism were needed to improve cooperation among SAARC members.
Sri Lanka's acting High Commissioner to India, Ramesh Jayasinge, said India's exports to Sri Lanka had grown by 300 percent in the past four years after Colombo started reducing tariffs.
"India has been one of the principal beneficiaries after Sri Lanka's tariff reduction," Jayasinge said.
He said Sri Lanka's economy would benefit more if dismantling of tariff barriers was done on a "sectoral basis" instead of a "product by product basis".
Jayasinge said wide scope existed for Sri Lanka's rubber component industry to increase exports to India to cater to India's rapidly growing automobile industry.
